acceleration: The rate at which an object's velocity changes over time; a vector quantity measured in m/s².
acceleration due to gravity, g: The downward acceleration of a freely falling object near Earth's surface, about 9.8 m/s².
apex / highest point: The top of a thrown object's path, where vertical velocity is zero but acceleration is still g.
arctangent: The inverse tangent function, used to find a direction angle from the ratio of vector components.
area under the curve: On a velocity-time graph, the area between the line and the time axis equals displacement.
area under v-t graph: The area between a velocity-time graph and the time axis, which equals the object's displacement.
average speed: Total distance traveled divided by the time taken; a scalar that is always zero or positive.
average velocity: Displacement divided by the time taken; a vector that includes direction and may be negative.
average velocity for const. acceleration: For constant acceleration, the average of initial and final velocity: v̄ = (v₀ + v)/2.
component: The projection of a vector onto a coordinate axis, such as its x or y part.
deceleration: A decrease in speed that occurs when acceleration points opposite to the direction of motion.
displacement: The straight-line change in position from start to finish; a vector that can be negative.
distance: The total length of the path an object actually travels; a scalar that is never negative.
free fall: Motion under gravity alone, ignoring air resistance, with the same acceleration g for any mass.
gravitational acceleration, g: The acceleration of a freely falling object near Earth, about 9.8 m/s², directed downward.
horizontal component: The sideways part of a velocity or motion; in projectile motion it stays constant since acceleration is zero.
initial / final velocity: The velocity at the start (v₀) and end (v) of the interval being analyzed.
initial velocity, v₀: The velocity of an object at the moment motion analysis begins.
instantaneous velocity: The velocity at a single instant, equal to the slope of the position-time graph at that point.
kinematic variable list: The five quantities (Δx, v₀, v, a, t) used to describe constant-acceleration motion.
launch angle: The angle between the launch direction and the horizontal; range is greatest at 45°.
launch velocity: The initial velocity when a projectile is thrown, resolved into horizontal and vertical components.
magnitude: The size of a quantity or vector, without regard to its direction.
maximum height: The highest point of a projectile's path, where its vertical velocity equals zero.
position: The location of an object given as a coordinate relative to a chosen origin.
position-time graph: A graph of position versus time whose slope at any point represents velocity.
projectile motion: Two-dimensional motion under gravity alone after launch, tracing a parabolic path.
pythagorean theorem: For a right triangle, the hypotenuse squared equals the sum of the squares of the other two sides.
range: The horizontal distance a projectile travels from launch point to landing point on level ground.
reference axis: The line from which angles are measured, usually the positive x-axis.
resultant vector: The single vector obtained by adding two or more vectors together.
scalar: A physical quantity fully described by magnitude alone, such as distance, time, or speed.
sine / cosine: Trigonometric ratios that relate an angle to a vector's components; cosine to the adjacent side, sine to the opposite.
slope: The ratio of vertical change to horizontal change on a graph, representing a rate of change.
slope of v-t graph: The slope of a velocity-time graph, which equals the object's acceleration.
slope of x-t graph: The slope of a position-time graph, which equals the object's velocity.
speed: The distance traveled per unit time; a scalar quantity with no direction.
stopped vs. instantaneous v = 0: A point where velocity is momentarily zero, which does not always mean the object is at rest.
symmetry of free fall: In air-free free fall, rise time equals fall time and launch speed equals landing speed.
time of flight: The total time from launch to landing, determined by the vertical motion.
time-independent equation: The kinematic equation v² = v₀² + 2aΔx, which contains no time variable.
uniformly accelerated motion: Motion in which acceleration stays constant in both magnitude and direction over time.
vector: A physical quantity that requires both magnitude and direction, such as velocity or force.
vector addition: Combining vectors by adding their components to find the resultant vector.
vector resolution: The process of splitting a vector into mutually perpendicular components.
velocity: The displacement per unit time; a vector quantity that includes direction.
velocity at maximum height: At the top of an upward throw the velocity is zero, but acceleration is still g downward.
velocity-time graph: A graph of velocity versus time whose slope gives acceleration and whose area gives displacement.
vertical component: The up-and-down part of motion, which accelerates at −g as in free fall.
action-reaction pair: Two equal and opposite forces, described by Newton's third law, that act on two different objects.
angle of incline, θ: The angle a ramp makes with the horizontal, which sets the gravity components mg sinθ and mg cosθ.
angle of repose: The incline angle at which an object just begins to slide, where tanθ equals μs.
atwood machine: Two masses connected by a string over a pulley, used to study acceleration and tension.
centrifugal force: A fictitious outward force that appears only in a rotating reference frame.
centripetal acceleration: The center-directed acceleration of an object in circular motion, equal to v²/r.
centripetal force: The net center-directed force keeping an object in circular motion, equal to mv²/r.
coefficient of friction, μ: A dimensionless number describing the roughness between two surfaces, with static and kinetic versions.
coefficient of kinetic friction, μk: A dimensionless constant that determines the kinetic (sliding) friction force.
coefficient of static friction, μs: A dimensionless constant that determines the maximum static friction force.
component of gravity: On an incline, the parts of gravity along the slope (mg sinθ) and perpendicular to it (mg cosθ).
constraint force: A force, such as normal force or tension, determined by a condition that restricts motion.
contact force: A force that acts only when two objects touch, such as normal force or friction.
contact vs. non-contact force: Contact forces require touching, while non-contact forces like gravity act across a distance.
direction of friction: Friction always acts opposite to the object's actual or attempted direction of motion.
equilibrium: A state in which the net force on an object is zero, so it stays at rest or moves at constant velocity.
external force: A force applied from outside an object that can change its state of motion.
fictitious force: An apparent, non-real force that seems to appear only in a non-inertial (accelerating) frame.
force: An interaction that can change an object's state of motion, measured in newtons (N).
force decomposition: Splitting a single force vector into two perpendicular components, often along and across an incline.
free-body diagram: A diagram showing all the forces acting on a single object as labeled arrows.
free-body diagram, fbd: A sketch of one object showing every force acting on it as a vector arrow.
friction force: A force at a contact surface that opposes the relative motion or sliding of objects.
gravitational force: The attractive force acting between any two objects that have mass.
inclined plane: A flat sloped surface that makes an angle θ with the horizontal.
inertia: An object's tendency to resist changes to its state of rest or uniform motion; greater for larger mass.
inertial reference frame: A non-accelerating frame, at rest or moving at constant velocity, in which Newton's laws hold directly.
interaction: A relationship in which two objects exert forces on each other.
kinetic friction: The constant friction force on a sliding object, equal to μk times the normal force.
kinetic friction, f_k: The friction force on an already-sliding object, f_k = μk·N, directed opposite to its motion.
mass: The amount of matter in an object and a measure of its inertia, measured in kilograms.
maximum static friction: The largest static friction force just before sliding begins, equal to μs times the normal force.
net force: The vector sum of all the forces acting on an object.
net force along incline: The net force directed along a ramp, mg sinθ minus any friction force.
net force, σf: The vector sum of all forces on an object; if zero the acceleration is zero, otherwise it produces acceleration.
newton, n: The SI unit of force; one newton accelerates one kilogram at one m/s² (1 N = 1 kg·m/s²).
newton's 2nd law: The net force on an object equals its mass times its acceleration: ΣF = ma.
newton's 3rd law: When object A pushes on B, B pushes back on A with an equal and opposite force.
newton's first law: An object stays at rest or in uniform straight-line motion unless acted on by a net force.
newton's second law: The net force on an object equals its mass times its acceleration (ΣF = ma).
newton's third law: For every action force there is an equal and opposite reaction force on the other object.
non-inertial frame: An accelerating reference frame in which fictitious forces seem to be needed.
normal force: The force a surface exerts on an object perpendicular to that surface.
normal force on incline: The perpendicular support force from a ramp, equal to mg cosθ in the simple case.
normal force, n: The support force a contact surface exerts perpendicular to itself, whose size depends on the situation.
reaction to normal force: The downward force a book exerts on the table, the reaction to the table's normal force.
reference frame: The coordinate system of an observer used to measure motion.
static friction: A variable friction force on a stationary object, up to a maximum of μs times the normal force.
static friction, f_s: The adjustable friction on a non-moving object that grows until it reaches μs·N, then sliding begins.
system approach: Treating two connected objects as one system to find acceleration from external forces, ignoring internal tension.
tension: The pulling force transmitted along a rope or string.
tension, t: The pulling force a rope, string, or cable exerts on an object, equal at both ends of a massless rope.
uniform circular motion: Motion in a circle at constant speed.
weight: The gravitational force on an object, W = mg, measured in newtons.
weight, w: The downward gravitational force on an object, W = mg, which changes where g changes.
average vs. instantaneous power: Average power is total work over total time, while instantaneous power is P = Fv at an instant.
collision: An interaction in which two objects exert large forces on each other for a short time.
conservation of energy: The total energy of a system stays constant even as it changes from one form to another.
conservation of mechanical energy: When only conservative forces act, the sum of kinetic and potential energy stays constant.
conservation of momentum: In a system with no external net force, total momentum is conserved before and after a collision.
conservative force: A force whose work depends only on start and end positions, not the path, such as gravity.
elastic collision: A collision in which total kinetic energy is conserved.
elastic pe: The energy stored in a stretched or compressed spring, equal to ½kx².
elastic potential energy, pe_spring: The energy stored in a deformed spring, PE = ½kx², proportional to the square of the deformation.
energy bar chart: A tool that uses bars to show the kinetic and potential energy at each point of a process.
energy transformation: The conversion of energy from one form to another while the total amount stays constant.
force-time graph: A graph of force versus time whose area equals the impulse delivered.
gravitational pe: The energy stored by an object's height, equal to mgh.
gravitational potential energy, pe_grav: The energy of a mass at height h in a gravitational field, PE = mgh, relative to a chosen reference level.
impulse: The product of force and the time over which it acts; equal to the change in momentum.
impulse-momentum theorem: The net impulse on an object equals its change in momentum: J = Δp = m(v_f − v_i).
impulse, j: The momentum change delivered when a force acts over time, J = FΔt, measured in N·s.
inelastic collision: A collision in which some kinetic energy is lost.
isolated system: A system with no external forces, in which total momentum is conserved.
joule, j: The SI unit of energy and work; one joule equals one newton-meter (1 J = 1 N·m).
kinetic energy: The energy an object has due to its motion, equal to ½mv².
kinetic energy loss in collision: The kinetic energy lost in an inelastic collision, converted into sound, heat, and deformation.
kinetic energy, ke: The energy of a moving object, KE = ½mv², proportional to mass and to the square of its speed.
loss of mechanical energy: The drop in mechanical energy caused by non-conservative forces doing negative work.
mechanical energy: The sum of an object's kinetic energy and potential energy.
momentum: The product of an object's mass and velocity; a vector measured in kg·m/s.
momentum, p: The product of mass and velocity, p = mv; a vector pointing in the direction of motion.
negative work: Work done by a force that has a component opposite to the displacement, removing energy.
net work: The total work done by all forces, equal to the work done by the net force.
non-conservative force: A force, such as friction, whose work depends on the path taken, so mechanical energy is not conserved.
nonconservative force: A force like friction or air resistance whose work depends on the path traveled.
perfectly elastic collision: A collision in which both momentum and total kinetic energy are conserved.
perfectly inelastic collision: A collision in which the objects stick together and move with one common velocity afterward.
positive vs. negative work: Work is positive when force aligns with motion and negative when it opposes motion.
potential energy: Energy stored by an object's position or deformation.
power: The rate at which work is done, P = W/t, measured in watts.
power, p: The amount of work done or energy transferred per unit time, P = W/t, measured in watts.
ramp length: The distance measured along the surface of an incline, which differs from its vertical height.
reference height: The level chosen as zero potential energy, kept consistent throughout a problem.
sliding distance: The actual distance over which two surfaces slide against each other in contact.
spring constant, k: A measure of a spring's stiffness, measured in N/m.
thermal energy: Energy generated by friction, equal to the friction force times the sliding distance.
watt, w: The SI unit of power; one watt equals one joule per second (1 W = 1 J/s).
work: The energy transferred when a force acts through a displacement, W = Fd cosθ, measured in joules.
work by perpendicular force: When a force is perpendicular to the displacement, the work it does is zero.
work-energy theorem: The net work done on an object equals its change in kinetic energy: W_net = ΔKE.
work, w: The energy transferred when force F moves an object through displacement d, W = Fd cosθ.
amplitude: The maximum displacement of a wave from its equilibrium position, related to its energy.
antinode: A point on a standing wave where the amplitude of vibration is greatest.
apparent frequency, f': The frequency an observer actually hears, which can differ from the source frequency.
beat: A periodic rise and fall in loudness when two waves of slightly different frequencies interfere.
boundary condition: A requirement specifying whether each end of a medium must be a node or an antinode.
calorimeter: An insulated device used to measure heat exchange, so heat lost equals heat gained.
closed pipe: A pipe closed at one end, supporting only odd harmonics with frequencies fn = nv/4L.
constructive interference: When two waves meet crest-to-crest, combining to produce a larger amplitude.
crest: The point of maximum upward displacement on a wave.
decibel, db: A logarithmic unit of sound intensity level, β = 10 log(I/I₀), where a 10 dB rise means ten times the intensity.
destructive interference: When the crest of one wave meets the trough of another, reducing the combined amplitude.
doppler effect: The change in observed frequency when a source or observer moves relative to the other.
energy transfer: What a wave carries from place to place; it moves energy, not matter.
first law of thermodynamics: The change in a system's internal energy equals heat added minus work done by it: ΔU = Q − W.
frequency, f: The number of oscillations per second, measured in hertz (Hz).
fundamental & harmonics: The fundamental is the lowest standing-wave frequency, and harmonics are its integer multiples.
fundamental frequency: The lowest frequency at which a standing wave forms, corresponding to n = 1.
harmonic: A frequency that is an integer multiple of the fundamental frequency.
heat, q: Energy transferred between systems because of a temperature difference, measured in joules.
interference: The pattern produced when two waves overlap and combine.
internal energy, u: The total kinetic and potential energy of all the molecules in a system.
longitudinal wave: A wave in which the medium vibrates parallel to the direction the wave travels, like sound.
medium: The material through which a wave travels; its particles only vibrate in place.
node: A point on a standing wave where the displacement is always zero.
observer velocity, v_o: The speed of the observer, which enters the Doppler effect calculation.
odd harmonics: Odd-numbered multiples of the fundamental frequency, produced only in a closed pipe.
open pipe: A pipe open at both ends, supporting all harmonics with frequencies fn = nv/2L.
oscillation: Repeated back-and-forth motion about an equilibrium position.
path difference: The difference in distance traveled by waves from two sources to a given point.
period, t: The time taken for one complete oscillation, equal to the reciprocal of frequency (T = 1/f).
phase difference: The amount by which two waves are out of step with each other.
reflection: The bouncing back of a wave at a boundary, where the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection.
refraction: The bending of a wave as it changes speed entering a new medium.
resonance: The large increase in amplitude when a driving frequency matches a system's natural frequency.
shock wave: A cone-shaped wavefront formed when a source moves faster than the wave speed.
sonic boom: The loud explosive sound heard when a shock wave passes an observer.
source velocity, v_s: The speed of the sound source, which appears in the Doppler effect denominator.
specific heat capacity, c: The heat needed to raise one kilogram of a substance by one kelvin, in J/(kg·K).
speed of sound, v: The speed at which sound travels through a medium, about 343 m/s in air.
standing wave: A fixed amplitude pattern formed by two equal waves traveling in opposite directions.
superposition principle: When waves overlap, the displacement at each point is the vector sum of their individual displacements.
supersonic: Faster than the speed of sound.
temperature, t: A measure of the average translational kinetic energy of a substance's particles, measured in kelvin.
thermal expansion: The increase in an object's size as rising temperature increases molecular vibration.
timbre: The quality or color of a sound, determined by its combination of harmonics.
transverse wave: A wave in which particles vibrate perpendicular to the direction of travel.
trough: The point of minimum displacement on a wave.
wave: A traveling disturbance that transfers energy without moving the medium itself.
wavelength, λ: The distance between two neighboring points in phase on a wave, such as crest to crest.
charge: The basic property responsible for electric interactions, measured in coulombs (C).
charge velocity, v: The speed of a moving charge, which determines the magnetic force it experiences.
coulomb's constant, k: The proportionality constant in Coulomb's law, about 9×10⁹ N·m²/C².
coulomb's law: The force between two point charges, F = kq₁q₂/r², proportional to the product of charges.
cross product: A vector product that gives a vector perpendicular to both inputs, as in v×B.
current: The rate at which charge flows, measured in amperes (A).
electric field: The force per unit positive charge at a point, E = F/q, measured in N/C.
electric field lines: Lines showing the direction and strength of an electric field, pointing from positive to negative.
electric potential: The potential energy per unit charge at a point, V = PE/q, measured in volts.
electric potential energy: The potential energy a charge has due to its position in an electric field, PE = qV.
equipotential line: A line connecting points of equal electric potential, always perpendicular to field lines.
equipotential surface: A surface of equal potential where no work is needed to move a charge along it.
equivalent resistance: The single resistance value that can replace a combination of resistors.
field strength: The strength of an electric field, shown by how closely the field lines are spaced.
force on a wire: The force on a current-carrying wire in a magnetic field, F = ILB sinθ.
inverse-square law: A relationship in which a force decreases in proportion to the square of the distance.
junction / node: A point in a circuit where current splits or combines.
kirchhoff's current law: At any junction, the total current flowing in equals the total current flowing out.
kirchhoff's voltage law: The sum of the voltage changes around any closed loop in a circuit is zero.
magnetic field from current: The magnetic field around a current-carrying wire, B = μ₀I/(2πr).
magnetic field, b: The field that carries magnetic force, measured in teslas (T).
magnetic force: The force on a moving charge in a magnetic field, F = qvB sinθ.
negative charge correction: For a negative charge, the magnetic force points opposite to the right-hand rule result.
ohm's law: The relationship between voltage, current, and resistance: V = IR.
parallel: A circuit connection where resistors share the same voltage and 1/R_eq = Σ(1/R).
point charge: An idealized charge treated as having no size.
potential difference, δv: The difference in electric potential between two points, also called voltage.
resistance: A measure of how much a component opposes the flow of current, measured in ohms (Ω).
right-hand rule: A rule using v×B to find the direction of magnetic force on a positive charge.
series: A circuit connection where resistors are in one line, sharing the same current and R_eq = ΣR.
solenoid: A coil of many wire loops that produces a uniform magnetic field inside.
test charge: A small positive charge placed to measure an electric field without disturbing it.
volt, v: The SI unit of electric potential; one volt equals one joule per coulomb (1 V = 1 J/C).
voltage: The potential difference that drives current through a circuit, measured in volts.
work by electric force: The work done as a charge moves through a potential difference.
